newsitem.title: USA: US Q2 growth still seen above potential-Fed source.
newsitem.headline: US Q2 growth still seen above potential-Fed source.

text.p: The incipient slowdown seen in the second quarter is not expected to be enough to bring U.S. economic growth to long-term sustainable levels, a source at the Federal Reserve said.

"I think it probably is true that the most recent data suggest the economy is slowing down after the rapid growth we saw in the early part of the year," the source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

"(But) I think the economy is still extremely robust. The growth rate may be slowing down but the level of economic activity is still very strong....It's just not growing as fast as it was a month or so ago," the source added.

The source said second quarter growth rates were expected to stay between 2.5 percent and 3.0 percent if the revised Gross Domestic Product (GDP) figures for the first quarter confirm the brisk pace previously reported.
First quarter economic expansion was first reported at 5.6 percent. The second estimate for first quarter GDP will be released on Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Wall Street economists, in a Reuters survey conducted last Friday, expected, on average, GDP to be revised to a 6.0 percent pace of growth in the first three months of the year.
The Fed source went on to say that even if the economy slows to 2.5 and 3.0 percent in the second quarter, "it would still be pretty good growth."

The source said some current Fed forecasts predict GDP growth of between 2.5 and 3.0 percent for the third and fourth quarters of the year as well, which would imply a growth rate of around 3.0 percent for all of 1997.
Is that sustainable?

"No. I don't think 3.0 percent is sustainable ... It may work this year but I don't think it would work for another year. I don't think it's sustainable for a prolonged period of time," the source said, "At some point the economy has to slow down."
The source said certain factors are working to slow the economy naturally after seven consecutive years of expansion.
Among those factors, the source pointed to the maintenance of a strong dollar, which was likely to take a toll on U.S. exports, and recent strong demand for durable goods.
"At some point those guys are going to say: 'We have enough cars, enough equipment,'" the source said.
The Fed source also commented on a thorny issue currently being discussed by policy makers -- the difficulties in gauging productivity gains in the economy.
The source said firms have been investing in new computer technologies for about 10 years, but still the expected gains in productivity were not entirely reflected in the economic data.

"It may well be that there is productivity growth going on but we're not able to capture it. To make the Fed's job easier, we have to have faster productivity growth that we can actually measure," the source said.
"The (question) is: If there is productivity growth that we're missing, then we're underestimating potential growth, but we're also underestimating actual growth," the source added.

The central bank source said some attempts to revamp the country's productivity indicators are being considered. One of the main suspicions at the Fed today is that the economy might be experiencing strong productivity gains in the service sector, which is "extraordinarily difficult to measure," the source said.
A study on the matter was recently conducted by the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the source said.

The research paper analysed productivity growth by industry. Basic findings of the survey showed a horde of industries where almost no productivity growth was taking place, according to official numbers.
"But just casual observation would make you think: There must be growth productivity going on," the source said.

"For example, I remember, according to the official numbers, there was no productivity (gains) in medical care. Well, you only have to walk into a hospital or a physician's office now and compare it to what it was like 10 years, 20 years ago, and you notice there is indeed productivity," the source said.
